subject: math

objective.text: Use the formulas for the area and perimeter of rectangles.

explanations.title: Perimeter by tracing and adding
explanations.text: Perimeter is the distance around a rectangle. Trace the outside and count the units. Or add the lengths of all four sides.

explanations.title: Formulas for perimeter
explanations.text: Opposite sides are equal. So you can double the length and double the width. Or add the length and width, then double that sum.

explanations.title: Area as rows and a formula
explanations.text: Area is the number of square units inside. Count the squares. Or skip count the rows. Or multiply length times width.

explanations.title: Finding an unknown side
explanations.text: For perimeter, take away the known sides and share the rest. For area, divide the area by the known side.

explanations.title: A table of whole number sides
explanations.text: One area can come from many rectangles. List each pair of whole numbers that multiply to the area. Then find each perimeter.

explanations.title: Length units and square units
explanations.text: Perimeter is a length, so it uses units like centimeters. Area counts squares, so it uses square units like square centimeters.

examples.title: A 4 by 7 rectangle
examples.text: The rectangle is 4 units wide and 7 units long. Its perimeter is 22 units. Its area is 28 square units.

source_ref.section: Concept Development, Problem 1 (S: 22 units; 4 units times 7 units is 28 square units)

examples.title: Perimeter of a 3 by 9 rectangle
examples.text: Add 3 plus 9 to get 12. Double 12 to get 24. The perimeter is 24 units.

examples.title: Area of a 3 by 9 rectangle
examples.text: Nine rows of 3 squares make an array. Multiply 9 times 3. The area is 27 square units.

examples.title: Two ways to check perimeter
examples.text: A rectangle is 2 wide and 4 long. Add 2 plus 4 to get 6, then double it to get 12. Or double 2 and double 4 to get 4 plus 8, which is 12.

source_ref.section: Concept Development, Problem 2 (S: both formulas give 12 units)

examples.title: Unknown length from the perimeter
examples.text: The width is 5 and the perimeter is 26. Two widths make 10. The other two sides make 26 minus 10, which is 16. Each length is 8.

examples.title: Unknown width from the area
examples.text: The area is 50 square centimeters and the length is 10 centimeters. Divide 50 by 10. The width is 5 centimeters.

examples.title: Rectangles with area 24
examples.text: Four rectangles work. They are 1 by 24, 2 by 12, 3 by 8 and 4 by 6. Their perimeters are 50, 28, 22 and 20.

source_ref.section: Concept Development, Problem 4 (derived: 2 x (1+24)=50, 2 x (2+12)=28, 2 x (3+8)=22, 2 x (4+6)=20)

hints.text: Perimeter is the distance around the rectangle. Think about all four sides.
Add the length and the width. Then double the sum.
Opposite sides are equal. Write all four sides, then add them.
Area counts the squares inside. Think of rows of squares, or length times width.
A square has four equal sides. Use the same number twice.
Think of the number that makes the product. Check it by multiplying.
Subtract the sides you know from the perimeter. Share what is left between the matching sides.
Area equals length times width. Divide the area by the side you know.
Find pairs of whole numbers that multiply to the area. Then check the perimeter.
Think about what you did in the lesson. Use math words in your answer.
